meta.label: Credit cards
meta.attribution: Covers the United States market: general-purpose credit cards issued by banks and credit unions, plus the routes that are not a rewards card at all. Interest rates on individual cards change with the prime rate and with marketing offers, so this comparison does not score them; it scores the two facts printed on a card's own terms that hold steady between updates, the annual fee and the ongoing rewards rate, on a 0 to 100 scale set by Conscious Consuming from the published figure (no annual fee scores 100 and the score falls as the fee rises; a higher ongoing cash-back-equivalent rate scores higher). Where a card's real risk is its interest rate rather than its fee, that is said in the description rather than folded into a score it was not built to carry: store cards and cards built to rebuild credit typically carry a much higher annual percentage rate than the general-purpose cards here, and a source is given for that. Complaint counts come from the CFPB Consumer Complaint Database, searched directly for each named company for credit card product complaints received January 2024 through December 2025; these are raw counts, not adjusted for how many cards an issuer has out, so a large national issuer will show more complaints than a small one even if its rate of trouble is no worse. Not financial advice. Reviewed 2026-08. Dispute or correct any rating via Contribute.

products.name: Store or retail credit card
products.brand: issued by a bank on a retailer's behalf
products.description: A card branded for a single retailer, usually offered at checkout with an instant discount, and usually issued behind the scenes by one of a small number of banks rather than the retailer itself. The CFPB found that four banks, Synchrony, Citi, Capital One and Bread Financial, issue over 80 percent of retail cards by outstandings. These cards typically charge no annual fee, but carry a far higher interest rate than general-purpose cards, which matters to anyone who does not pay the balance in full.

fees.note: The CFPB's Issue Spotlight on retail credit cards describes them as typically carrying no annual fee, unlike their finding on interest rates. The same report states that in December 2024, new retail cards offered by the top 100 retailers had an average private label APR of 32.66 percent, compared with an average general-purpose card APR of 25.2 percent that year, and that 90 percent of retail cards reported a maximum APR above 30 percent, compared with 38 percent of general-purpose cards.

products.name: Become an authorized user on someone else's card
products.description: Instead of opening a card, a person is added to a family member's or partner's existing account. The CFPB describes an authorized user as distinct from a joint account owner, and states that being an authorized user generally does not obligate that person to repay the account's debt. The account's payment history can be reported to the authorized user's own credit file, which is why the route is sometimes used to help a person with no credit history build one, but it depends entirely on the primary cardholder's own behaviour on the account.

fees.note: An authorized user does not hold the account and is not billed an annual fee in their own name; any fee is the primary cardholder's.

products.name: Debit card, no credit card at all
products.description: Spending directly from a bank or credit union account rather than borrowing. The CFPB describes a debit card as a way to spend money already in an account: a transaction is denied rather than allowed to become debt, and unless the account is overdrawn there is no repayment and no interest charge. It carries none of the rewards or purchase protections a credit card advertises, and does not build a credit history.

fees.note: The CFPB states that with a debit card you are spending money you already have in your account, generally cannot spend more than the account holds, and unless you overdraw the account you do not need to repay money or pay fees, unlike a credit card where you are borrowing and must repay by the due date or face a late fee and interest charges.
